title: Java Collections Revision Notes
summary: Quick revision of the Java Collections Framework: the List, Set, Map and Queue hierarchies, ArrayList vs LinkedList, HashMap and TreeMap internals, sorting with Comparable and Comparator, safe iteration and generics basics.

chapters.title: Collections Hierarchy Mental Model
points: Collection extends Iterable; List, Set and Queue extend Collection, but Map does NOT extend Collection
List: ordered, indexed, allows duplicates (ArrayList, LinkedList)
Set: no duplicates; HashSet (unordered), LinkedHashSet (insertion order), TreeSet (sorted)
Queue/Deque: FIFO and double-ended access; ArrayDeque, LinkedList, PriorityQueue (heap order, not FIFO)
Mistake: iterating a PriorityQueue or HashSet and expecting sorted/insertion order

chapters.title: ArrayList vs LinkedList
points: ArrayList is a resizable Object[]: get(i) is O(1), add at end is amortized O(1), insert/remove in the middle is O(n) due to shifting
Growth: ArrayList grows by about 1.5x when full, so pass an initial capacity when the size is known
LinkedList is a doubly linked list: get(i) is O(n), add/remove at a known node or at either end is O(1)
Comparison: ArrayList wins for random access and memory (cache-friendly); LinkedList has per-node overhead and is rarely faster in practice
Mistake: calling list.remove(int) vs list.remove(Object) on a List<Integer>; remove(1) removes the index, not the value

chapters.title: HashMap Internals
points: HashMap is an array of buckets; index = (n-1) & hash(key.hashCode()), with default capacity 16 and load factor 0.75
Resize doubles the table and rehashes when size exceeds capacity x load factor

Collisions chain as a linked list; a bucket converts to a red-black tree once it holds more than 8 entries (TREEIFY_THRESHOLD = 8) and the table has 64 or more buckets, otherwise the table resizes instead, giving O(log n) worst case
get/put are O(1) average; equals() and hashCode() must be consistent: equal objects must have equal hash codes
Mistake: mutating a key after insertion, or overriding equals without hashCode, makes the entry unfindable
HashMap allows one null key; Hashtable and ConcurrentHashMap do not

chapters.title: TreeMap and Map Variants
points: TreeMap is a red-black tree: keys kept sorted, get/put/remove are O(log n)
Navigation methods: firstKey, lastKey, floorKey, ceilingKey, headMap, tailMap, subMap
LinkedHashMap keeps insertion order (or access order for LRU caches via removeEldestEntry)
Comparison: HashMap O(1) unordered, LinkedHashMap O(1) ordered, TreeMap O(log n) sorted
Mistake: TreeMap uses compareTo/compare for key equality, not equals, and disallows null keys

chapters.title: Comparable, Comparator and Safe Iteration
points: Comparable: natural order defined inside the class via compareTo(T o), one order per class
Comparator: external order via compare(a, b); build with Comparator.comparing(Person::getAge).thenComparing(Person::getName).reversed()
Comparison: Comparable is the class's single default order; Comparator supplies many orders without changing the class
Removing elements inside a for-each loop throws ConcurrentModificationException; use Iterator.remove() or list.removeIf(...)
Mistake: compare via subtraction (a - b) can overflow; use Integer.compare

chapters.title: Generics Basics and Cheat Sheet
points: Generics give compile-time type safety: List<String> avoids casts; type arguments must be reference types (List<Integer>, not List<int>)
Type erasure: generic types are erased at runtime, so List<String> and List<Integer> are the same class
Wildcards: ? extends T for reading (producer), ? super T for writing (consumer), known as PECS
Cheat: ArrayList for default lists, ArrayDeque for stacks/queues, HashMap/HashSet for lookup, TreeMap/TreeSet for sorted, PriorityQueue for min-heap
Cheat: use List.of/Set.of/Map.of for immutable collections; they throw UnsupportedOperationException on modification
